claim.pdf_says: Third column of the 8.9 reserved-word list ends: FLOAT-BINARY-32 / FLOAT-BINARY-64 / FLOAT-BINARY-128 / FLOAT-DECIMAL-16
claim.why_it_matters: FLOAT-DECIMAL-16 falls out of the reserved-word table as a loose paragraph. The word is still present, but a tool that harvests the reserved-word list from the table cells would miss it.

verdict.reasoning: The 300-dpi render of printed page 167 (PDF page 191) shows the third column of the 8.9 list ending FLOAT-BINARY-32, FLOAT-BINARY-64, FLOAT-BINARY-128, FLOAT-DECIMAL-16. The first and second columns are one line shorter (they end at CHARACTER and DIVISION). page-191.md holds the table through '| CHARACTER | DIVISION | FLOAT-BINARY-128 |' and then FLOAT-DECIMAL-16 as a line directly after it. The claim quotes both sources accurately, but no word is missing: FLOAT-DECIMAL-16 is still in the transcription, in the same position and the same order. The 8.9 list is a flat list of words; its three columns are layout, and the column a word sits in carries no meaning. What differs is table layout only: the last row of a ragged column was not given its own row of cells. A reader of the transcription loses nothing. The risk to a tool that reads only table cells is a tooling concern, and that tool should be checked against the word list. It is not a content discrepancy between the PDF and the markdown.
